details.title: More about the project
details.lead: How the thing behind the buttons actually works — no marketing promises.

items.title: What a "breakdown" actually is, and why it's this detailed
items.text: The reference goes into Gemini whole — as a YouTube link or a file. What comes back is a structure: timestamped scenes with headings, cast members with a description of their look and role, extras kept separate from the cast, visual style, pacing, aspect ratio, plus an assessment of the video's audience and what it's selling. A breakdown isn't a summary — it's the raw material the prompt is later built from: every piece of it can be dropped, edited or replaced.

items.title: Why relevance is scored separately
items.text: A winning video isn't universal — it worked for its own audience. A separate check compares who the reference is aimed at with who buys your product — by age, gender, interests, category and price tier — and answers with a 0–100 score, the reasoning behind it, a list of mismatches, and concrete prompt edits. Sometimes the honest answer is: pick a different reference.

items.title: The brand manifest — set once, used in every video
items.text: Style, tone, voice-over voice, recurring characters and locations are described once and plugged into every video of the brand. A session gets a copy of the manifest at launch time: edits inside a video don't change the brand itself, and changing the brand doesn't retroactively rewrite what's already been made.

items.title: What the model sees as an image, and what as words
items.text: Veo accepts no more than three reference images. The service shows exactly which three will be sent — characters, your scenes, brand scenes, product photo — and lets you assemble that set by hand. Anything that doesn't make the slots is described in the prompt as text instead of being lost.

items.title: The library of breakdowns and privacy
items.text: The breakdown of every public video is saved and offered to others as a ready-made scenario — making a repeat analysis unnecessary. Breakdowns of videos uploaded as a file are private: only the author sees them, and they never appear in shared results. Under the terms of use, breakdowns themselves are the service's intellectual property; your product, your materials and the finished video remain yours.

items.title: Files and how long they're kept
items.text: References, product photos, frame captures and finished videos live in Vercel Blob. Every file has an owner in the database, and deleting the owner deletes the file: an expired session takes its files with it, a deleted product takes its photo, a deleted manifest takes its character and scene photos. Daily cleanup is backed up by a separate sweep for orphaned files.

items.title: Browser and Telegram — one app
items.text: The same product opens as a regular website and as a Telegram Mini App, with no difference in capabilities. An anonymous session works without signing in; signing in through Telegram is needed for projects, the product catalog, the brand manifest and any plan above Lite — those are tied to a user.

items.question: Do I need to sign up?
items.answer: No. The session is anonymous and created automatically on your first visit — you only need to accept the public offer and terms of use once, before your first breakdown. Signing in through Telegram is available but optional: it's needed for projects, the product catalog, the brand manifest, and to come back to your sessions later.

items.question: Which video formats are supported?
items.answer: MP4, MOV and AVI up to 100MB, or simply a link to a public YouTube video — in which case there's nothing to download or upload at all.

items.question: How long does video generation take?
items.answer: Once the prompt is approved, the video is usually ready in 3–5 minutes — the time depends on the chosen mode (Fast or Standard) and current load on Veo 3.1.

items.question: How much does it cost?
items.answer: Right now, nothing: all three plans — Lite, Standard and Premium — are free and switch right inside the app. This is a rollout period; whatever you've already made stays yours once paid plans arrive. Later, Lite is planned to become conditionally free — in exchange for liking the project's YouTube channel and sending a few links to the service.

items.question: What's the difference between the plans?
items.answer: Lite is the minimal path: reference breakdown and video generation in 16:9 or 9:16. Standard adds a relevance check, a video artifact audit, a brand manifest, your own scenes, photo character swap, any aspect ratio, and publishing. Premium is Standard plus the library of ready-made breakdowns. You can switch plans at any time without affecting projects, videos or breakdowns you've already made.

items.question: Where are my files stored, and when are they deleted?
items.answer: In Vercel Blob — the reference, product photos and the finished video all live in the same storage. Every file has an owner in the database: an expired session takes its files with it, a deleted product takes its photo, a deleted manifest takes its character and scene photos. Cleanup runs daily, and a separate pass picks up orphaned files.

items.question: Who owns the breakdowns and the finished videos?
items.answer: The service creates the reference breakdown, and under the terms of use the breakdowns belong to it — that's exactly what lets the library offer them to other users. Your product, your uploaded materials and the generated video remain yours. Breakdowns of videos uploaded as a file are private: only the author sees them.

items.question: Can I use it from Telegram?
items.answer: Yes — the same product works both as a regular website in a browser and as a Telegram Mini App inside Telegram, with the same set of features.

items.question: Can I manually edit the video breakdown or the prompt?
items.answer: Yes, at both steps: after the automatic reference analysis and after the automatic prompt generation, both results can be edited before moving on.

items.question: Is this an open-source project?
items.answer: Yes — the source code is available on GitHub, and development followed the GitHub Spec Kit methodology.
